profile.title: AES Recommended AES70 Microphone Profile
profile.purpose: Define one agreed set of AES70 control objects for microphones, so that a controller which knows the profile can operate any compliant microphone without vendor-specific knowledge. AES42 already standardises what a remotely-controlled microphone can do; AES70 standardises how any audio device is controlled. X230 is the bridge: it takes each AES42 parameter and binds it to a specific AES70 class, sitting at a specific role inside a specific reusable block, carrying its value in a specific property.

source.transcribed: Every parameter below is a row of the Classes sheet. `source_row` is that row number, so any entry can be checked against the workbook.

narrative.heading: What the profile is
body: X230 is a draft AES recommendation that describes a microphone as a set of AES70 (OCA) control objects. It is not a wire format and not a specification sheet — it is a control model. It answers one question: when a controller connects to a microphone and wants to change the pad, where does it look?

The workbook that carries the model is a two-column translation. The left half is AES42 — the existing standard for digitally-controlled microphones, whose parameters are named in the language of microphone engineering: preattenuation, polar pattern, low-cut, polarity inversion. The right half is AES70 — the control architecture, whose language is classes, blocks, roles and properties. Each row is one parameter carried across.

narrative.heading: The logic: a four-part binding
body: Every parameter in the profile is pinned down by four things, and it is the combination that makes it findable rather than any one of them.

The **class** says what kind of control it is — OcaSwitch for a discrete selector, OcaGain for a continuous level, OcaMute for on/off, OcaFilterClassical for a fixed-shape filter. The class also decides the semantics: an OcaSwitch has numbered positions with names, so a pad becomes positions whose names are gain values.

The **block** says where in the device it lives. AES70 blocks are reusable groupings; X230 names four for the audio path — Preamp, Processor, Utility, ADC — and six for radio gear. Device identity is not in a block at all: it hangs off the device manager.
The **role name** is the label the object carries inside its block, and it is what a controller actually searches for: role 'Pad' in block 'Preamp'.
The **property** is the field on that class holding the value. OcaSwitch carries it in Position, OcaGain in Value, OcaMediaClock in RatesSupported and CurrentRate.

So 'the pad' resolves to: OcaSwitch, in the Preamp block, at role Pad, read and written through Position — and the profile adds that the position *names* are the gain values, which is what lets a controller show '-10 dB' instead of 'position 2'.

narrative.heading: Blocks and the signal chain
body: The blocks follow the signal, not the enclosure. Preamp holds everything that happens to the analog signal before conversion — pad, pattern selection, low-cut, gain, polarity, mute, and the rated sensitivity. Processor holds the DSP that follows conversion — compressor, EQ, limiter, delay. ADC holds conversion itself: sample rate, word length, and the latency the conversion costs. Utility holds what is not in the signal path at all — the identify light and the test-signal generator.

This is why the block matters as much as the class. OcaGain appears twice in the profile: once at role Gain in Preamp, and once at role BoosterGain in the radio blocks. Same class, different meaning, told apart only by where it sits.

narrative.heading: The radio half
body: The second half of the Classes sheet is a separate collection, gathered for wireless equipment. It is structured differently: instead of naming one block per parameter, it marks each parameter against six device roles — Transmitter, Receiver, Analyzer, Manager, transmit antenna and receive antenna — with 'y' where the parameter applies and 'm' where it may.

That grid is the interesting part. Frequency select applies to all four active devices and may apply to the antennas; RF mute and RF output power apply only where there is a transmitter; SWR applies where there is something to measure standing waves against. Reading down a column gives the object list for one class of radio device.

narrative.heading: How an object list is written
body: The workbook's Help sheet defines the convention for listing a real device's objects: one header row per object, then one row for each element of that object worth documenting — basic functional properties, read-only properties whose read-only status matters, elements that are unimplemented or partially implemented, and elements with semantics an ordinary controller would not expect.

Each row is typed. O marks an object; P a property; R a read-only property; M a method; E an event; and N an element that is *not implemented* — the code exists so that a device can positively declare an optional element missing, rather than leaving a controller to guess. Indent depth carries nesting: the root block one notch, objects inside it two, and so on. Items an ordinary application should not see are flagged ADV.
The N code is the reason this repository's device view distinguishes 'absent' from 'unknown'. The profile itself takes the position that a missing element is a fact to be recorded, not a gap.

narrative.heading: State of the draft
body: The workbook is marked DRAFT, revision 01, dated 2018-05-02, and it shows. Four parameters have no class assigned: Stereo ('not in focus at the moment'), Type ('what is this, exactly?'), RF link test features and external filter band (both 'tbd'). The Blocks sheet — which was to carry each block's name, ID and purpose — contains only its column headers; no block was ever filled in, so block identity in this transcription is derived from the Block column of the Classes sheet and from the block diagrams.

There are two smaller slips worth knowing about, both preserved with notes: the Sensitivity row has its role name and property swapped relative to every other row, and the polar-pattern position table skips position 9, jumping from 8 (short shot gun) to 10 (long shot gun).

blocks.name: Preamp
blocks.purpose: The analog front end: everything done to the signal before conversion, plus the microphone's rated sensitivity.

blocks.name: Processor
blocks.purpose: Signal processing after conversion — dynamics, equalisation, delay.

blocks.name: ADC
blocks.purpose: Analog-to-digital conversion and its clock: sample rate, word length, and conversion latency.

blocks.name: Utility
blocks.purpose: Functions outside the signal path — the identify light and the test-signal generator.

blocks.name: Device
blocks.purpose: Device-level identity carried by OcaDeviceManager rather than by any block: manufacturer, serial number, user label.
blocks.notes: The workbook writes 'n/a' in the Block column for these rows, meaning they are not inside a reusable block.

blocks.name: Analyzer
blocks.purpose: A spectrum analyser or scanning receiver used for coordination.

blocks.name: Manager
blocks.purpose: A management device coordinating a set of radio links.

blocks.name: Xmit Antenna
blocks.purpose: A transmit antenna, where it is itself controllable.

blocks.name: Rcv Antenna
blocks.purpose: A receive antenna, where it is itself controllable.

diagrams.title: Smart mic
diagrams.summary: The full model: one microphone containing the entire chain, from capsule to whichever output the manufacturer fits. Everything downstream of the ADC is digital, and the output stage is a choice rather than a fixed design — analog via DAC and line amp, AES3, network audio over IP as AES67, or a radio transmitter. Control arrives separately as AES70 over IP and fans out to a control point in every stage.

diagrams.title: Simple wireless mic
diagrams.summary: The same chain cut back to what a body-pack or handheld transmitter actually contains: transducer, attenuator, preamp, ADC with its clock, transmitter, antenna. There are no filters, no dynamics and no output choice — the radio link is the output. A receiver and its antenna are drawn alongside because the transmitter still has to be told what to do, and network control reaches the microphone through them.

diagrams.title: Base station
diagrams.summary: The receiving half, and the mirror image of the smart mic: the chain starts at the antenna instead of the capsule. RF comes in to a receiver, then filters and dynamics, then the same set of output options — analog, AES3, network audio — plus clocking as its own controllable block. A transmitter sits alongside for the return link back to the microphone.

polar_pattern_position.description: Positions of the OcaSwitch at role PatternType. The workbook gives them as position number and standard pattern name; the parenthesised figure is the first-order gradient coefficient, which is what the companion PatternParameter object carries.

statuses.label: Mapped
statuses.description: The catalogue supplies a value for this profile parameter.

statuses.label: Absent
statuses.description: The catalogue positively records that the device does not have this function — the equivalent of the profile's own 'N' type code.

statuses.label: Unknown / NULL
statuses.description: The parameter applies to this device but the catalogue holds nothing that could answer it. The value is null.
